scope_note: Free public programs, nonprofits and official locators for families raising children and young adults with autism, ADHD, developmental, learning, physical, medical or behavioral health disabilities. Private therapy providers are not listed. Contacts come from published official or organization sources and are not telephone-confirmed.

resources.name: CDC milestone checklists and Milestone Tracker app
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Free checklists show what most children do at each age, from 2 months to 5 years. They come in English and Spanish, and there is a free phone app.
resources.how: Fill out the checklist for your child's age. Take it to your child's next doctor visit. You do not need a diagnosis to ask for help.

resources.name: Find your state's early intervention program
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Every state has free early intervention for children under 3 who are behind or have a disability. You can call yourself. You do not need a doctor's note.
resources.how: Look up your state's number and ask for a free evaluation. If your child is 3 or older, call your public school district instead.

resources.name: Your state's Parent Training and Information Center
resources.org: Center for Parent Information and Resources
resources.what: Every state has a free parent center for families of children with any disability, from birth to age 26. Staff help with school plans, meetings and your rights.
resources.how: Find your state on the map. Call before your next school meeting.

resources.name: Family-to-Family Health Information Center
resources.what: Parents who have been there help other families with doctors, insurance, Medicaid and disability services. There is one in every state.
resources.how: Find your state's center on the map and call or email them.

resources.name: Parent to Parent: get matched with another parent
resources.what: A trained volunteer parent whose child has a similar disability calls you, listens and shares what helped them. It is free.
resources.how: Find your state's Parent to Parent program on the map and ask to be matched.

resources.name: Autism Society National Helpline
resources.what: Trained staff help families find autism services, support groups and local chapters. This is not a crisis line.
resources.how: Call on a weekday or fill out the online form. Ask about the chapter in your state.

resources.name: National Down Syndrome Society
resources.what: Information and support for families of people with Down syndrome at every age, including a free guide for new and expecting parents.
resources.how: Call or email, or download the new-parent guide.

resources.name: Learning Disabilities Association of America
resources.what: Information for parents on dyslexia and other learning disabilities, evaluations and school help. More than 30 states have a local chapter with support groups and advocacy help.
resources.how: Read the parent section and check whether your state has a chapter.

resources.name: Hands & Voices
resources.what: A parent-led group for families of children who are deaf or hard of hearing. It supports every communication choice and has state chapters, including Ohio.
resources.how: Start with the new-families page and find the chapter near you.

resources.name: FamilyConnect
resources.org: American Printing House for the Blind
resources.what: Free information, parent stories and an online parent support group for families of children who are blind or have low vision.
resources.how: Visit the website and join the online parent community.

resources.name: National Resource Center on ADHD helpline
resources.what: A helpline answers questions about ADHD: diagnosis, treatment, school help and local support groups. Spanish speakers are available.
resources.how: Call the ADHD helpline, or use the parent toolkits on the website.

resources.name: NAMI Basics and the NAMI HelpLine
resources.what: NAMI Basics is a free 6-week class for parents and caregivers of children and teens with mental health symptoms, taught by parents who have been there. It is offered in person or online. The HelpLine gives information and support. It is not a crisis line.
resources.how: Find a class through your local NAMI or take the online version. Call the HelpLine on weekdays.

resources.name: SSI for children with disabilities
resources.what: Monthly payments for children with serious disabilities in families with low income and savings. In most states, SSI also means Medicaid. At 18, Social Security checks again using adult rules.
resources.how: Start online or call for an appointment. Have medical and school records ready.

resources.name: National Respite Locator
resources.what: Respite gives family caregivers a short break while someone trained cares for your child. This search finds respite programs and ways to pay for them.
resources.how: Search by state. The list is not complete, so also ask your county or state disability office.

resources.name: Sibshops for brothers and sisters
resources.what: Fun peer-support events for school-age brothers and sisters of kids with disabilities and health needs, offered in most states, plus online groups for teen and adult siblings.
resources.how: Use the website to find a Sibshop near you.

resources.name: Choices besides guardianship at 18
resources.org: National Resource Center for Supported Decision-Making
resources.what: At 18, your child legally makes their own decisions. Guardianship is not the only option. Supported decision-making lets your child choose trusted people to help with decisions while keeping their rights.
resources.how: Read about the options before you go to court. Ask your parent center or disability rights agency for help.

resources.name: Help Me Grow Early Intervention
resources.org: Ohio Department of Children and Youth
resources.what: Ohio's free early intervention for children under 3 who are behind or have a disability. It is in all 88 counties, and visits usually happen at home. Parents can sign up their own child.
resources.how: Call or fill out the online form, and a local coordinator will call you. If your child is almost 3, call now. This program ends at age 3, and the school district takes over.

resources.name: Faster autism evaluations close to home (ADEP)
resources.org: OCALI, Help Me Grow and the Ohio Department of Developmental Disabilities
resources.what: In many Ohio counties, local doctors and early intervention staff work as a team to evaluate young children for autism sooner, without a long wait for a big hospital.
resources.how: Ask Help Me Grow or your child's doctor if an ADEP team serves your county.

resources.name: Nisonger Center at Ohio State
resources.what: A university center in Columbus with clinics that evaluate children, teens and young adults for autism and other developmental disabilities, including mental health concerns.
resources.how: Call to ask which clinic fits your child's age and how to get on the schedule.

resources.name: Children's hospital evaluations for autism and development
resources.what: Ohio's large children's hospitals have teams that check children for autism, developmental delay and complex ADHD. These visits often have a wait of several months, so it helps to get on the list early.
resources.how: Ask your child's doctor for a referral. Most hospitals then call you to set the visit. Keep using Help Me Grow or the school while you wait. Your child does not need a medical diagnosis to get those services.

locations.name: Cincinnati Children's Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics
Cleveland Clinic Children's Center for Autism

resources.name: Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD)
resources.org: Ohio's Parent Training and Information Center
resources.what: Ohio's free parent center for families of children with any disability, from birth to 26. Staff explain evaluations, school plans and your rights. Based in Marion.
resources.how: Call before an evaluation or school meeting, or when you disagree with the school.

resources.name: Ohio Family to Family and Parent to Parent
resources.what: Ohio parents who have been there give free help with doctors, insurance and Medicaid. Ohio Parent to Parent can also match you with a trained parent mentor for one-to-one support.
resources.how: Call or email, or ask to be matched with a parent mentor.

resources.name: Ohio Parent Mentors
resources.what: Parent mentors are parents of children with disabilities. They work with schools to help other families through special education.
resources.how: Ask your school district or educational service center if a parent mentor serves your area.

resources.name: Ohio special education: information for families
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Ohio's guide to special education for families: evaluations, school plans, parent rights and where to get help.
resources.how: To ask for a free evaluation, write to your school district's special education director. Keep a copy and write down the date you sent it.

resources.name: Autism Scholarship Program
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Pays for special education from approved providers for children whose school district has found autism and written an IEP.
resources.how: Read the parent information. Then check with your district that your child's IEP lists autism before you apply.

resources.name: Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Pays for special education from approved providers for children with an IEP. The amount depends on the child's disability.
resources.how: Read the program page, or email peterson.scholarship@education.ohio.gov with questions.

resources.name: OCALI (Ohio Center for Autism and Low Incidence)
resources.org: Funded by the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Free guides, training and a lending library for families of children with autism and other less common disabilities, from early childhood into adulthood.
resources.how: Start with the family section of the website.

resources.name: Help for Ohio children who are deaf or hard of hearing
resources.org: Ohio School for the Deaf statewide services
resources.what: The Ohio School for the Deaf helps families and local schools across the state, not just its own students. Ohio Hands & Voices and parent mentors who know hearing loss are also available.
resources.how: Read the state's list of programs, then ask your school district or Help Me Grow to connect you with statewide services.

resources.name: Ohio State School for the Blind outreach
resources.org: Ohio State School for the Blind
resources.what: Serves children from birth to 21 who are blind or have low vision. Besides its school in Columbus, it helps families and local schools across Ohio with materials, training and advice.
resources.how: Call to ask about outreach for your child and your school district.

resources.name: Your county board of developmental disabilities
resources.what: Your county board is where local services for developmental disabilities start. It decides who qualifies, assigns a helper to plan services, and runs Medicaid waivers and family support money.
resources.how: Find your county on the map, or call the state line and ask to be connected to your county.

resources.name: Ohio Medicaid for children
resources.what: Health coverage for children in families who qualify, including checkups, therapies and mental health care. Children with disabilities may also qualify through SSI or a county board waiver.
resources.how: Apply online at benefits.ohio.gov, by phone, or at your county Job and Family Services office.

resources.name: CHADD of Ohio parent support group
resources.what: A free online group for parents of children with ADHD, run by Ohio's CHADD chapter. Topics include feelings and self-control, school and homework, daily routines, and taking care of yourself. Cincinnati and Toledo also have local branches.
resources.how: Find CHADD of Ohio on CHADD's chapter list and sign up for the next meeting. The group has met online on the third Thursday of each month at noon.

resources.name: OhioRISE
resources.org: Ohio Department of Medicaid with Aetna Better Health of Ohio
resources.what: A Medicaid program for children and young people up to age 20 with serious mental health or behavior needs. It adds a care coordinator plus in-home and crisis help.
resources.how: Ask your child's Medicaid plan, doctor or counselor whether your child should be checked for OhioRISE.

resources.name: Youth mobile crisis team (MRSS)
resources.org: Ohio Department of Behavioral Health and Ohio Medicaid
resources.what: Free crisis help that comes to your child, for anyone 20 or younger in any Ohio county. A trained team, including a licensed counselor, can usually arrive within an hour at home, school or another safe place. You decide if it's a crisis.
resources.how: Call or text 988 and ask for MRSS. If anyone is in physical danger, call 911.

resources.name: County Family and Children First Council
resources.what: When a child's needs involve several agencies at once, such as school, mental health, the county board of DD or children services, your county council can bring everyone to one table to make one plan. Some councils can also help pay for things like respite or mentoring.
resources.how: Call your county's Family and Children First Council and ask for service coordination. Families can ask for it themselves.

resources.name: Complex Medical Help (formerly Children with Medical Handicaps)
resources.what: Helps pay to diagnose and treat certain long-term medical conditions, and connects families with approved doctors. It was called Children with Medical Handicaps.
resources.how: Call the public health nurse at your county or city health department to start.

resources.name: STABLE Account (Ohio's ABLE account)
resources.what: A savings account for people with disabilities. Money saved here does not count against SSI or Medicaid limits the way a regular bank account does.
resources.how: Read about the program or call the STABLE team before you open an account.

resources.name: Planning for 18: decision-making toolkit
resources.what: A free 2026 toolkit for young people with disabilities and their families. It explains supported decision-making, powers of attorney and other choices that are less restrictive than guardianship.
resources.how: Go through the toolkit with your teen before 18. Call Disability Rights Ohio with questions.

resources.name: Pre-Employment Transition Services
resources.what: Free help for students with disabilities, starting at age 14: exploring jobs, work experience, job skills, speaking up for yourself and college planning.
resources.how: Ask your child's IEP team or transition coordinator to request these services from OOD.

resources.name: Resolving special education disagreements
resources.org: Ohio Department of Education and Workforce
resources.what: Ohio's advice for settling disagreements with the school early: talk to the special education director, get help from a parent mentor or parent center, and ask for a guided meeting or mediation.
resources.how: Read this before you file a complaint. Keep copies of every letter and email.

resources.name: Military OneSource special needs consultations
resources.what: Free consultants help military families with special education, TRICARE, EFMP and local services. Retirees and honorably discharged members can use it for one year after leaving service.
resources.how: Call any time or start a chat to set up a phone or video meeting.

resources.name: Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP)
resources.what: Active duty families sign up a family member with special medical or school needs. This helps the military plan moves and support around those needs. Some TRICARE programs require it.
resources.how: Contact the EFMP office at your base, or call Military OneSource.

resources.name: TRICARE Extended Care Health Option (ECHO)
resources.what: Extra TRICARE benefits for active duty families whose child has a qualifying disability: training, special education, equipment, home health care and respite for the main caregiver.
resources.how: Call your TRICARE regional contractor to sign up. Services must be approved before they start.

resources.name: TRICARE Autism Care Demonstration
resources.what: TRICARE's way to pay for ABA therapy for children with autism, with no yearly or lifetime limit. Active duty families must also join EFMP (unless excused) and sign up for ECHO.
resources.how: Follow the steps on the TRICARE page. You will be given an autism services navigator to help.

resources.name: STOMP: Specialized Training of Military Parents
resources.what: The parent center for military families of children with disabilities, in the U.S. or overseas. Its workshops and webinars are open to all military-connected families.
resources.how: Call, or look up the next online workshop.

resources.name: CHAMPVA health coverage for veterans' children
resources.what: Health coverage for children of veterans rated permanently and totally disabled by a service-connected condition (or who died from one), if the family cannot get TRICARE. It usually ends at 18, or 23 for full-time students. A child who could not support themselves before 18 may stay covered.
resources.how: Check if you qualify and apply on VA.gov, or ask your county veterans service officer to help.

DC.name: Disability Rights DC at University Legal Services

changes.title: Federal special education oversight is moving
changes.text: In June 2026 the U.S. Department of Education announced it is moving day-to-day oversight of special education to the Department of Health and Human Services, and civil rights enforcement to the Department of Justice. The law has not changed: your child still has the right to a free public education and an IEP, and your school district and state are still responsible.

changes.title: TRICARE autism coverage is under review
changes.text: A national study recommended making ABA therapy a regular TRICARE benefit instead of a pilot program, and senators have asked the Defense Department to act. Check TRICARE's page for the current rules before you sign up.

changes.title: Ohio may recognize supported decision-making in law
changes.text: Senate Bill 35 would recognize supported decision-making as an alternative to guardianship for adults with developmental disabilities. The Ohio Senate passed it unanimously; it is now in a House committee. Supported decision-making can already be used today. The bill would add a standard state form and legal protections.

glossary.plain: Testing to see if your child has a delay or disability and what help they need. Early intervention and public schools do this for free.
Free help for children under 3, usually at home, such as speech or physical therapy and coaching for parents.
A written school plan for a child who needs special education. It lists goals, services such as speech therapy, and supports. Parents are part of the team that writes it.

A written school plan for a child with a disability who does not need special education but needs changes to learn, such as extra test time or breaks. A child who does not qualify for an IEP may still get a 504 plan.
A therapy often used for autism that teaches skills step by step. Insurance, Medicaid and TRICARE rules for it vary.
In Ohio, the county office for developmental disabilities. It decides who qualifies and helps plan and pay for services.
A Medicaid program that pays for help at home and in the community, such as aides or respite, for people who qualify.
Supplemental Security Income: monthly payments from Social Security for people with disabilities who have low income and savings.
A savings account for a person with a disability that does not count against SSI or Medicaid limits.
A court gives another adult the right to make decisions for a person 18 or older. It removes some of that person's rights, so less restrictive options are worth looking at first.
The young adult keeps their rights and chooses trusted people to help them understand choices and make decisions.
The part of an IEP, starting by age 14 in Ohio, that plans for life after high school: work, school and living.
Short-term care that gives family caregivers a break.
The military's Exceptional Family Member Program for active duty families with special medical or school needs.
Mobile Response and Stabilization Services: Ohio's free youth crisis teams. Call or text 988 and ask for MRSS.
